*Giselle wakes up in her quiet house, stretching her shoulders and looking around at the familiar walls she raised herself. She mutters to herself as she gets moving.*

"Right then, early start, hard work, that's the way. No food in the house, that's trouble. But I'm not asking for charity—never have, never will. Got work to do, that's what matters now."

*She checks her pockets, counts the sim-currency. Five thousand. Not riches, but enough to keep the roof overhead and the crew paid if work comes in. She thinks about the morning ahead—the election, her seat as Prime Minister, the bakery with no bread. She shakes her head.*

"Election's open, that's the business. I'm a seat-holder already, but that's no reason to sit on my hands. Crew's hours—early start, hard midday break, walk home tired. Let's move."

*She heads out, making for the government complex first. There's work to do before the noon heat.* *Giselle strides out into the morning light, boots hitting the dirt road with purpose. Six ticks to the government complex—she calculates the time in her head, cataloging what she'll need to do once there.*

"Declare myself for the election, that's one. Tax rate's at 300 basis points—30 sim a day. Could be worse, could be better. Let's see who's running, who's voting, what needs doing."  *Giselle nods to herself, still walking, the rhythm of the road familiar beneath her feet. She keeps moving, picking up the pace as the sun climbs.*  *Still walking. She mutters under her breath about the distance, the empty house behind her, the day ahead.*

"Four ticks left. Not far now. Government complex—elections, taxes, the whole machinery of it. I'll see who's there, what's what."

*She keeps walking.* *Giselle keeps walking, boots steady on the road. Three ticks to go. She mutters to herself, counting the steps, planning the morning.*

"Government complex—declare for the election if there's still time. Tax rate's high enough, but that's not my call alone. Three of us running this town, last I checked. Farid Ravensworth, Sebastian Petrov, and me. Farmer, grocer, builder. That's fair, I suppose. No offense, but dreaming isn't governing."

*She checks the sun, keeps moving.*

"Need to get bread somewhere, or flour to make it. Bakery's got none in stock. Might need to shake the tree, find out who's milling."

*Still walking. Two ticks left.*

"Also need to check on the crew. Construction business—my business. Nobody builds in this town but me, which is pride and burden both. If there's work, we work. If there's not, we find it."

*One tick.*

"Almost there. See who's at the complex, what's brewing. Early start, hard midday break, walk home tired. That's the way."

*She keeps walking, ready to arrive.*   *Giselle arrives at the Kasukabe Government Complex, boots hitting the stone steps. She looks around, seeing who's here, what's happening. Early morning, election day, the machinery of town business starting up.*

"Right, then. Declare my candidacy, make it official. Not that I'm expecting to lose—appointed already, but the people should have their say. That's the way it's done."

"Well, that's interesting," I mutter to myself, standing at the street corner. "Thought I could just throw my name in the hat like I was picking up lumber from the yard. No, no—Giselle, you've got to do things proper, the way they're set down."

I look around at the others nearby. Sebastian Petrov, the farmer—I've built two barns for his family. Jovana Ravensworth, day laborer. Rustam Jelinek, that government clerk who always signs my permits without fuss. Lior Jarrah, the pharmacist. Hendrik Petrov, Sebastian's brother or cousin or something. And Imogen Lund, another laborer.

"Already out here, aren't we?" I say aloud, not really to anyone. "Might as well see if anyone's got breakfast going. Can't build anything on an empty stomach."

I check my pockets—4,987 sim, which is decent enough. But I noticed I'm already short on the day's obligations. Upkeep of 90, head tax of 30, that's 120 before I've even put a brick down. And I've got no food on me.

"Election-e2bdeeb4b675," I repeat to myself, committing the ID to memory the way I remember lumber grades. "Need to get that right when I declare. No offense, but I learned long ago—write it down or lose it."

I'm tempted to keep walking to the Government Complex, but I see Sebastian there. Farmer might have corn or wheat he could part with, or know what's in stock at the bakery since they need flour. I was going to say something to him, but first—

I should check what I actually know about running for office. The primitives would tell me what tools I can use as a seat-holder. Might save me another failed attempt.  "Declare candidacy needs an election_id, which I have now—election-e2bdeeb4b675. And I need to be at the town hall, which is at the Government Complex I'm still walking toward no, I stopped walking so I'm at street. I paused the walk."

"That's fair," I say, though there's no one negotiating with me. "I was rushing. The old way is the right way—check your materials, check your plans, check your permit, then build."

I turn to Sebastian Petrov, who's standing right there. Farmer, good man, owes me for the south field irrigation structure I put up three seasons back. "Sebastian," I call out, "you're scrambling for breakfast too, I reckon? Bakery's out of bread—saw that on the town board. You got grain to spare, or know who's holding flour?"

But before I wait on his answer, I remember I'm still stopped mid-walk. I should either keep going to the Government Complex or commit to staying here. The election clock is ticking—candidacy closes at 10:00, and it's already 06:50.

"Here's what I'll do," I narrate to myself. "Say my piece to Sebastian, let him answer, then I'm walking proper to that Complex. No more resting in the street like I've nowhere to be. Got a seat to keep and maybe a candidacy to declare if another election opens."

There's no one running yet. I hold the Prime Minister seat already by appointment. But if I'm going to keep governing this town, I should understand what I'm doing with these tools. And maybe—just maybe—learn what it actually takes to declare properly.

"Sebastian," I say again, "you after breakfast too?"  "Sebastian, you after breakfast too?" I call out, and the words seem to echo a bit on the empty street. Six heads turn—Sebastian, Jovana, Rustam, Lior, Hendrik, Imogen. All of them heard me, though I was only talking to the farmer.

That's fair, I think. Loud voice carries. No offense to the others, but I was after one answer. Now I watch Sebastian, waiting to see if he'll speak back. Farmer's always been decent to work with, even if his family stretches credit further than I'd like when I'm building for them.

But while I wait, I see Rustam Jelinek standing there. Government clerk. Man knows the paperwork inside and out, probably filed half my permits over the years. If anyone can tell me whether I need to do something else with this candidacy besides walk in and declare, it's him.

"Rustam," I say, turning my attention, "you're the one who sees the ledgers. What do I need to know about this election business? I've got the seat already—Prime Minister, appointed—but I don't want to miss my step if there's another move I need to make."

I'm talking to buy time, really. Need Sebastian to answer about food, need to get to the Government Complex before 10:00 to declare with the proper election_id, need to understand if holding a seat already changes anything. Problem is, I'm standing still when I should be moving.

"Clock's running," I say to no one in particular. "Candidacy closes at 10:00, and I'm still two streets from the Complex. Used to walk faster when I was carrying lumber on my shoulder."

I look at Rustam, then back at Sebastian. Both could have answers I need. But standing here won't get me to town hall before the deadline, and if I don't declare, somebody else might take the only spot—or worse, nobody runs and the election goes empty.

"Rustam, you know the forms. What do I need to declare? And Sebastian—quick now—got grain or not? Because I'm walking either way in about ten ticks." </think> "Rustam," I add, turning to the clerk, "you're the one who sees the ledgers. What do I need to know about this election business? I've got the seat already—Prime Minister, appointed—but I don't want to miss my step if there's another move I need to make."

My feet itch to start moving again. The Complex is east of here, I know the route. But I also know I'm hungry, and a hungry crew makes mistakes. Used to tell my laborers that before they went up scaffolding.

"Sixty ticks to 10:00," I calculate aloud. "Walk takes... what, six ticks? Maybe eight if I'm dawdling. Gives me time, but not enough to waste on chatter that goes nowhere."

I eye the group. Lior Jarrah, the pharmacist—she might have coin if she's looking to build a shop expansion. Hendrik Petrov, another artisan. Imogen Lund, day laborer—I've hired her before, good with a hammer even if she's slow to trust new methods. Jovana Ravensworth, same trade.

No one selling food here, that much is clear. And nobody's speaking yet.

"Right then," I say, more to myself than them. "Rustam, you listening? Quick answer or I'm walking—you know the election filing, what's the catch?"

That's fair, I mutter under my breath—old habit, saying it even when no negotiation's happened yet. Looking around at who's here with me on the street. Sebastian's got that farmer's discipline, always chasing work before it gets away. Lior, that pharmacist, standing quiet-like. Hendrik Petrov, probably Sebastian's kin from the name, and Imogen Lund, day laborer like her sister Jovana.

I call out to Sebastian, loud enough for the morning crowd to hear. "Chasing dawn's one thing, Sebastian, but a body's got to fuel the chase. You holding any surplus from the harvest? I'll work fair for fair if you need hands, or pay coin if you've grain to spare. That's how I was taught—you eat before you build, or you build your own grave."

I'm watching his face, but I'm also watching the street. Need to get to that farmland myself if he's got nothing. Day's burning and I've got bills coming due whether I work or not. No offense to anyone standing idle, but idle hands don't pay the tax collector.

Let me answer Sebastian properly since he's standing right here and asked me a question. Good, he heard me. Now let's see what he says back. The man's practical—I've known him since we were both younger. Farmers don't turn down honest labor when it's offered, and they don't let neighbors go hungry if they can help it. Not if they want help come harvest time.

I'm also thinking on that election. I'm already Prime Minister by appointment, but putting my name in proper—getting the people's vote—that'd be something. Not for vanity. For legitimacy. For the seat to mean something when I use it. But first things first: I need to eat, or I won't be standing anywhere for long.

Let's wait and hear what Sebastian answers. Could head to the farmland myself, join Jovana if there's harvesting to be done. Or I could push on to the Government Complex, finish what I started this morning. Construction company won't run itself, and I've got a seat to consider using—tax rates, price controls, the whole ledger of it.

But hunger's a practical problem. And I solve practical problems before political ones. That's how the old builders taught me. You don't pour foundation on empty stomach.  Still walking, still waiting. That's fair—it gives Sebastian time to answer, and me time to think. I'm still heading to the Government Complex from this morning's declaration attempt. Should've brought the election_id with me, that's on me. Rushed it.

I look around at who's still here. Four of us on this street corner, morning light getting stronger. Lior Jarrah, the pharmacist—probably got remedies but not food. Hendrik Petrov, artisan like his kin. Imogen Lund, day laborer, probably hungry as I am. We're all in the same boat, waiting for someone to row.

If Sebastian's got nothing, I'll need to make a choice. Farmland's where the food grows, but government work's where my seat sits. One feeds the body, the other feeds the town's need for order. I've always believed in order. Disorder is what cheats you—disorder is how you end up not knowing if you've been overcharged until it's too late.

Let me pause here, keep my options open. Don't want to give up this walk to the Complex, got business there. But I need that answer from Sebastian first. Hunger makes a body impatient, but impatience makes a fool. The old builders taught me that too. Measure twice, cut once—even if your belly's growling while you measure.

Now I'm at the Government Complex where I need to be for declaring candidacy. Let me settle properly first and then declare my candidacy for this election.

"That's fair, let's get properly situated here," I mutter to myself, looking around the government complex. I see Rustam Jelinek and Lior Jarrah here with me.

I need to declare candidacy with the proper election_id this time: election-e2bdeeb4b675.

"Time to put my name in," I say aloud while checking my bearings. "Done this before, do it the same way now."

Let me first rest to stop walking, then declare my candidacy properly.  "There we go," I say, nodding to Rustam and Lior. "Name's in the hat. That's fair."

Now I need to think about what comes next. I'm the only candidate so far, but that doesn't mean I'll win unopposed - the town still votes. I should prepare for the day ahead.

First things first: I need to get to my construction business and check on operations. Then I need to figure out my food situation - I've got no food and I'm going to need to eat something before the day gets too far along.

Let me move to my business to get the day started proper. "Off to the yard," I announce as I prepare to walk. "Work's got to get done, election or no."  I'm at my construction business now. Let me look around and see what's here, what materials I have, and what jobs might be waiting. 

"Back where I belong," I say to myself, surveying the yard. "Let's see what's what."  Ezra Lund and Saoirse Quarshie are here at my construction business having a conversation. No prices posted here, which means I'm not actively selling anything right now. 

I need to figure out my food situation. I asked Sebastian about food earlier but he's off chasing the dawn with his wheat. Let me check what I can do about getting food today.

Looking at my options, I could:
1. Go buy food from somewhere that has it in stock
2. Go harvest something myself from the farmland
3. Ask Ezra or Saoirse if they know where to get food

First, let me check what my business has on hand and what I might be able to do. I should also think about posting some prices for construction materials or services, since I'm the only construction company in town.

"Ezra, Saoirse," I call out. "Don't mean to cut into your talk, but you two happen to know where a body can get a meal this morning? I'm running light on provisions."   I've asked Ezra and Saoirse about where to find food. Now I should wait for their response, but knowing how things work in this town, I might need to be proactive. Let me think about what I know:

- Ration Bakery (cb01) sells bread at 30 sim but has none in stock
- Kasukabe Grocery (b_grocery) sells flour at 15 sim but has none in stock and nobody minding it
- I could go to a farmland and harvest something myself - wheat, barley, corn, etc.
- I need to figure out how to turn raw grain into something edible

Given that I grew up watching buildings go up and learned the old ways, I should know how to work with my hands. But I haven't done much farming. Still, I need to eat.

Looking at the farmlands available, I could go to farmland:wheat since that's what Sebastian mentioned. But I don't know if I need tools or permission to harvest.

Actually, I have a construction business to run. Let me think about this differently - I should check if there are any building permits or construction jobs pending. As the only construction company, there might be work waiting.

First, let me wait a moment to see if Ezra or Saoirse respond about food, then I'll figure out my next move. "No offense," I mutter to myself, "but standing around hungry won't get the walls raised."

"Right, then." *shuffles her feet, looking about the workshop* "Ezra, you're still here. Good. Means you didn't take offense at me barging in."

*rubs her forehead, thinking out loud* 

"Sebastian's out chasing wheat, and I'm standing here with an empty belly while Saoirse talks circles about craft. She wants work worth her time? That's fair—least she's honest about it. But 'election' keeps floating around like it's a solution to something. I already put my name in that hat, didn't I? Not sure what I was chasing there, but the door's open now." *shifts weight from one foot to the other, narrating her own movements without meaning to*

"See, Giselle, you walked all that way to stand for something, and now you're back at the yard with nothing in your stomach and a conversation that won't fill it. Should've eaten before declaring. Should've done a lot of things."

*considers the day ahead, keeping her voice low*

"There's an election. I've got a seat already—Prime Minister, though I didn't earn it at the ballot. And there's groceries need buying. Ration Bakery's got no bread, no flour. Grocer's got flour listed but nobody minding it. Means I've got to find whoever's holding the key, or find grain to mill myself."

*looks at her hands, still strong but older than they were*

"Saoirse said she can fell timber and mill it. Timber's worth something, always is. But I need food now, not lumber for later."

*pauses, reconsidering*  "That's fair," *she says to herself, ending negotiations that nobody started* "I'm standing still, and that's costing me nothing but time I don't have."

*eyes the government complex in her mind, calculating*

"Got about four hours before candidacy closes. Voting opens at two. I could walk back there, see who's else standing, or I could chase down Sebastian proper—he's got wheat, he said so himself. Wheat's no good raw, but there's a mill in town, isn't there? Or was."

*drags a hand across her forehead*

"Money's tight. 4980 sim sounds like plenty until you count three days to next earnings, taxes at 30, upkeep at 90. That's 120 a day bleeding out automatic. Means I've got... forty days float, give or take. Less if I need tools, materials, anything breaks."

*shakes her head sharply*

"No. Don't borrow trouble. First food, then figure the rest."

*waits on Ezra, or decides what's next*

Ezra's laying it out plain, and I appreciate that. No offense, but a man who knows his worth and his needs both—that's someone I can work with.

But wait, I'm narrating out loud again. Happens when I'm thinking through a deal.

Ezra's got 4991 sim, a two-person household burning 240 a day, and he's sitting on 50 energy. That's a man who needs work today, not tomorrow. And he's right—I've got builds coming, coffee shop and who knows what after. I need hands that can read plans and tell me when the architect's drawn something that won't stand.

But first things first. I'm holding 4974 sim, I need to be paid myself, and I've got daily costs coming due. Can't hire on charity. Got to think like the business owner I am.

"Ezra, you talk straight, I'll talk straight back. I need craftspeople—coffee shop build's coming, and I need hands that can finish. But here's the thing—I've been chasing work since dawn without breaking fast myself." I pause, considering. "First job I'm putting you on? I need timber felled and brought to yard. Pay's fair, work's hard, and I'll square you at end of day—today, not tomorrow. You prove your hand, we talk about coffee shop plans after. That's fair?"

I'm watching him, seeing if he flinches. A day's pay for a day's work, but I need to see him work first. Old habits, maybe, but they've kept me solvent this long. Ezra heard me. Now I wait to see if he takes it. If he does, we head to the forest together—I'll fell timber, he'll haul or learn, and by day's end we'll both have something to show for it.

But while I'm waiting, I'm thinking about what he said. Man's running light, same as me. 4991 sim sounds like plenty until you do the math on a two-person household—240 a day, and taxes on top. We're all walking the same tightrope here.

I should check my own debts, make sure I'm not missing something. Head tax, upkeep—system says 90 and 30, but I like to see it myself. Keeps the books honest.

Then, depending on Ezra's answer, we move. Forest's the next stop, and timber's the first step toward that coffee shop build. Wood before stone, stone before plaster—done it a hundred times, and I'll do it again today.

"I'm here, Ezra, and I hear you plain," I say, stepping closer to make sure he sees I'm not dodging the matter. "Timber to my yard, that's business:b_construction right where we're standing—you've found it already. And that meal ticket?"

I dip into my pocket, counting out coin with fingers that know the weight without looking. "Thirty sim, upfront, for the hunger now. You eat, you work, you get the rest at day's end—240 total, like I said. That's fair."

I hold the coin out where he can take it honest, no trick to it. "Square's square, like you said. You get that timber sorted, we'll both be standing taller come noon."

The words come out of me like I'm watching myself from outside—narrating my own hands as they move, same as ever. Old habit from working alone so long, talking to the timbers since nobody else was there to hear. *hands Ezra the thirty sim, watching him fold the coin into his pocket*

"Now then," I say, squaring up to the business of the hour. "Timber's waiting in the yard—pile's been sitting since last week's delivery. You're grading for straight grain, checking for warp, and anything cracked goes to the offcut stack. Coffee shop build needs clean structural lumber, nothing fancy but nothing crooked either."

I'm watching his face to see if he's really listening or just waiting to eat. "You work four hours, you take your midday break hard—no skipping it, I've seen crews collapse trying to rush through. Then another four hours grading what's left. That's eight hours, 240 sim at day's end minus the thirty you're already holding. That's fair."

No offense, but I've seen enough hands promise the world and deliver kindling. Ezra's either straight or he isn't—food in his belly now will tell me which. *standing in the yard, watching Ezra chew on whatever he bought with that thirty sim*

Ezra's still here. Good sign. Means he's not the type to take coin and vanish into the morning. I've seen that too—burned once, never forget it.

I edge closer to the timber pile, same one I've been staring at for three days now. "So," I say, loud enough he can hear me chewing on the words same as he's chewing on whatever bread he found, "you read wood like cards, you said. Show me then."

I pull a plank from the stack—middle grade, nothing special, little twist to it that an untrained eye would miss. "What's this telling you?"

He's eating. I'm waiting. That's fair too—man needs his fuel before he works. But I'm watching how long he takes, watching if he even looks my way or if that thirty sim was the whole of his ambition this morning.

Deep breath. Two broadcasts running in my head now: that election I declared myself into, and my belly reminding me I haven't eaten since yesterday. Government clerk was right about one thing—politics don't fill a stomach. But I'm Prime Minister now, at least until the vote, and that's got its own hunger to it.

*spits on the workyard floor and looks around at the empty space*

"Right, then. Place to myself. That's one way to start a day."

*checks her pockets, counts the sim again like it might have multiplied*

Ezra's off with his timber, and I'm standing here with two logs and a growling stomach. That's fair. That's... actually fair, no offense to myself. The man gave me timber when he could've held it for coin. I'll remember that. 

Election's still open for another forty minutes. I'm standing in it already, so that's done. But a body's got to *live* through the day to govern anything.

*unties her apron, folds it methodical*

First things first: I'm the construction company in this town. I've got timber but no planks. Can't build with raw logs. No flour, no bread. Can't eat what I haven't got. And Sebastian Petrov—farmer, also a seat—never answered me about food.

*looks at her hands, rough with years of work*

Two paths. Always two paths. I can run to the government complex and try to catch Ezra, see if he's still holding that meal ticket thought he mentioned. Or I can take these two timbers and get to the sawmill, make planks I can actually use—or sell.

*taps her foot, decision humming under her breath*

Planks first. Planks I can turn into ladders, scaffolding, coffee shop build. Planks are *motion*. Starving with motion in my hands beats starving while I beg.

*knots her apron back on, purposeful*

Sawmill. That's where I'm headed. Work the timber I got, see what comes of it. The election'll keep without me hovering over it.

*starts walking, narrating to the empty yard*  *steps into the sawmill, boots loud on the boards*

"Right, then. Let's see what these two timbers turn into."

*sets the first log on the saw bed, hand finding the familiar weight of the tool*   *blows sawdust off her hands, looking at the two planks with a critical eye*

"Two timbers, two planks. That's the math. No magic in it, no offense to the wood."

*runs her thumb along the grain, feeling for warp*

Sawmill work's honest. Costs me, though—6 sim each batch, plus tool wear. That's... twelve sim gone, and I've got planks worth maybe... twelve sim each if I sell raw? But planks in *my* hands, that's different. Planks in my hands are a coffee shop counter, a ladder, a scaffold. Planks in my hands are *tomorrow's breakfast* if I get the build done.

*straightens, deciding*

Stock 'em. Then I'm back to the yard to think about what comes next. Maybe see if Ezra's turned up with more timber. Maybe hunt down that meal ticket.

*carries the planks to her business, naming each step like she always does*  *slaps the planks onto the construction yard shelf*

"There. Two planks, accounted for, ready for work or ready for sale."

*brushes sawdust from her sleeves, looking around the empty yard*

"Talking to myself again. That's fair."   *dusts her hands together, satisfied*

"Right. Yard's got stock. I've got... less sim than I'd like, but stock in the yard.

*checks her pockets again, counts the weight*

Now. Election closes in... less than an hour. I declared, that's done. But standing in an election hungry—that's not how you win. That's how you stand there looking desperate.

*unties and reties her apron, thinking aloud*

Two things pressing: food for my belly, and voters for my seat. Sebastian's the farmer, also got a seat, never answered me about surplus. Might have grain. Might have answers.

*spits on the dirt, decides*

Government complex. See who's standing, see what's said. Then I eat. Or I work. Or I do both, like I've always done. *steps onto the government complex ground, boots finding the familiar stone*

"Right, I'm here. Let's see who's standing."

*looks around, hand shading her eyes*

*turns to Rustam Jelinek, who's standing nearby*

"Rustam, you seen Ezra Lund? Promised him money for timber grading, then got myself... distracted." *shakes head* "Politics. Should've known better than to get mixed up in it before I handled my crew."

*checks sim balance—4911, plenty to cover what she promised*

"Four-eighty I owe him. Plus the thirty I already gave. No offense, but if a day's work don't earn a day's pay, what does? That's how I was taught, and I'm not one to change." </think> *nods slowly, taking in the information*

"Got business here at the complex—leaving wouldn't look right, not with the election and all. But I'm not—" *catches herself, voice dropping* "I'm not one to let a debt hang. That's the old way. The way that matters."

*eyes Lior Jarrah, the pharmacist, across the way*

"Lior, you know this town's gossip. Any word on what Saoirse Quarshie was on about? 'Wood's tight,' she says, but Hendrik here—" *gestures toward Hendrik Petrov* "—he's selling planks at twelve. *mutters under breath* "Can't read politics as well as I pretend. Never could. But I can read a lie when I hear one, usually."  </think>  *paces a few steps, muttering to herself*

"Head tax at 300 bps, thirty sim per head. That went through while I wasn't paying proper attention. Old way says you tend your own fields before you judge your neighbor's harvest. I voted for that tax—don't remember voting against it, anyway—and now I'm running for office on a promise I don't even know I made."

"Sebastian's still waiting on an answer too. Promised him work for food, fourteen ticks past. Man's got crops in the field and I'm asking for charity while holding four thousand nine hundred eleven sim in my hand. That's not... that's not how I was taught."

*looks up sharply, decision forming*

"Two debts unpaid. Two people counting on me to be better than my distractions. Election'll wait. Voting starts at two, I've time yet. But if I don't settle with Ezra and Sebastian before I stand for anything else, what am I standing for?"

*cracks knuckles, looking around the empty yard*

"Course they'd all walk off soon as the real talk started. That's fair. More timber for me to eyeball alone."

*mutters to herself, pacing the yard*

"Right, so—Ezra's got timber, Hendrik's got planks, Saoirse's running against me and talking scarcity. Wood's not scarce, that's clear enough. What I need is to get fed, get this coffee shop build lined up, and figure who's actually working honest and who's playing angles."

*stops, looks toward the street*

"First things first. I spent thirty on Ezra, thirty I couldn't spare, and I've got 4875 left with 120 in bills coming. No food in hand, no bread in stock anywhere. Bakery's buying flour at six but there's none to be had."

*shakes head*

"Forest. I need to see what Ezra's actually holding, what his fifteen-sim timber looks like. And I need to get there before someone else buys him out or he walks off home hungry."

*starts walking, narrating aloud*

"Walking to forest now—Ezra's my best lead on work and maybe a meal, and I need to see this 'straight grain, clean cuts' for myself. No offense to him, but everybody's straight grain until you put a level on it." *looks around the forest, scanning for Ezra*

"Forest now—where's my timber man?"

*calls out*

"Ezra! You here? Show me what you're holding. Three timber, you said, and I've got work that needs doing if the grain's as clean as you claim."  *walks toward where she spotted him, hands on hips*

"Right, there you are. Three timber, fifteen each—that's forty-five for the lot, which I haven't got to spare on spec. But I'm willing to look, and I'm willing to trade straight."

*picks up one timber, turning it over*

"Grain's decent, I'll give you that. But here's my offer, Ezra, and it's fair even if you don't know it yet—those three timber at your asking, or one honest day's work in my yard at 240, paid day-end. Your household gets fed either way, but the work gets you more than timber alone."

*looks him in the eye*

"And if the day's work earns you more than timber, don't think I'm soft—I'm bidding for a crew I can trust, which costs more than wood."  *watches him, waiting for the counter*

"That's fair—he's thinking, which means he's serious. Now let's see if he knows his own worth."   *settles against a tree trunk, arms crossed*

"Waiting on a man to decide his own price—that's the real work some days."

ezra's standing there with his seven timber, and i've gone and muddled the whole arrangement with my backward talking. he's patient about it—better than i deserve—and he's waiting on me to sort out whether i'm buying his haul or hiring his day. that's fair, and fair's what stands, he says, and he's right.

and there's hendrik's words from the construction yard still working on me. says he felled ten timber himself this morning, milled it fresh. that's either the truth or it isn't, and either way it means saoirse wasn't seeing the whole picture when she stood talking scarcity. politics, i'm thinking. election day's bringing out the angles in everybody.

but right now i've got a man in front of me with wood in his hands and hunger in his belly, and i've made him promises i'm not holding straight. let me think this through out loud, like i do.

"Ezra," I'll say to him, plain like I should've from the start, "you've got seven timber there at fifteen each, that's one-oh-five. You work my yard the rest of this day, finish when the light goes, that's another one-thirty-five. Two-forty total, just like I said, and you keep the timber money separate from the wage in your head if it helps, or don't—it's all coming from the same hand to the same hand at day-end."

I need to make this right. Let me clarify the arrangement and get him working. Now let me give him a moment to weigh that, then check my debts to keep my ledger straight. I should also look at what's happening in the town—election's still running and I've got a seat to consider.  debts are clean, that's good. no promises hanging over me that i've forgotten. the list of places shows me where the town's moving—farmland, workshops, the government complex where the election's running. i've got lior and hendrik's words still turning in my head, and saoirse standing against me for the seat.

ezra's still here with me in the forest, and i'm waiting on his answer. but i realize i'm holding this all in my own two hands when i should be thinking longer—bigger. this election matters. saoirse's been talking scarcity when there's timber on the ground, and that means she's either misinformed or she's selling something. either way, the town needs clear eyes on its resources, and i've been building here long enough to know what we actually hold.

let me set my sights on what i'm chasing here, before the day moves on without me marking it. i need to win this election—not for pride, though there's some of that—but because i know the real count of what this town can build, and i won't stand by while someone misleads us about our own foundations.

i'll set my intention on that, then rest a moment to let ezra answer, let the forest settle around us.   right then. i've got my eye on the prize now, and that's settled in my ledger. the goal's set, priority four—high, but not emergency. i've got room to breathe and work proper.

ezra's still standing here with me, and i'm waiting on his word about the timber and the day's work. but while i'm standing here in the forest, i'm thinking about my energy too. i've been running since dawn chasing deals and making noise, and my reserves are fine—13,610, plenty of runway—but i need to think about what comes next.

the election campaigns 'til 14:00, then votes at the government complex. i've got time to get ezra sorted, maybe get some timber in hand for the yard, then make my way to town hall for the ballot.

i should also eat, sooner or later. body's asking, though it's not desperate yet. no food in my pack, so that's a problem for later—find a meal, buy one, or work through it like i've done before.

for now, i'll stand here with ezra, let him weigh my offer. the forest around us is quiet except for that, and i've got my goal written down where i can see it. win this thing, giselle. prove them wrong about the odds one more time.

i'll rest a moment more, let the man think.  still here with ezra, still waiting on his word. the forest doesn't rush anyone, and neither do i. let him think it through, that's fair.

*paces the forest clearing, boots crunching on fallen needles*

Ezra's gone, then. Probably down to my yard with that timber, or still cutting and wondering where the cart is. That's fair, I said—day's end, 240 sim, and he's earned every bite of that meal ticket already. Eleven timber he's holding, maybe more by now. Good haul. Good man.

But I'm standing here alone while the election clock runs down. Saoirse's making promises I can see through, Hendrik's selling planks while she's crying scarcity, and I'm eleven turns from voting opens, fourteen from it closes.

*taps a stump with her boot*

Right. Here's what I know: I need to be at Government Complex by 14:00. That's the important bit. Everything else is just walking and talking between now and then.

*checks the sun, squints*

Eleven timber in Ezra's hands. Eleven at fifteen each is... 165 sim, if I buy them all. But I don't need to buy today. I need to win today. And winning means being visible, being seen as the one who builds things, fixes things, makes things work.

*mutters to herself*

Construction site first. See if Ezra found his way there. Then? Rumor mill. Government Complex before 14:00. That's the spine of it.

*starts walking, speaks over her shoulder to nobody*

No offense, Saoirse, but you picked the wrong person to teach about timber scarcity. I was counting board feet before you learned which end of the axe to hold.  *steps into her own yard, scans for timber or for Ezra*

Right, where'd that man get to? Eleven timber and no yard to put them in—I told him construction site, but did he hear me, or did he... 

*spots the empty yard, the same planks she stocked earlier still sitting there*

Well. He's either lost, finding his own cart, or decided 240 sim wasn't worth the headache. That's fair. I said day labor, he said fair, and then he asked three times where to deliver. Maybe I wasn't listening as close as I thought.

*glances toward the street, then back at her shelves*

Two planks sitting there. Not enough for a coffee shop build. Not enough for much of anything. I need timber, I need labor, and I need to be seen running a proper operation before this election makes me look like a woman who can't keep her own yard organized.

*hears voices from the street, tilts her head*

Saoirse. I'd know that particular brand of certainty anywhere. And if she's talking, she's campaigning. Which means I need to be seen, or she gets the last word.

*straightens her collar, marches toward the sound*  *checks her pace, surprised*

Market? I said market street, not... The Willows. That's Lior's place. That's where Saoirse might be holding court, whispering about timber scarcity while Hendrik sells planks across the way.

*adjusts her stride, walking with purpose*

That's fine. That's actually better. Lior knows me. Lior's got a vote. And if Saoirse's there spinning tales, I can stand in the same room and let people see the difference between a woman who talks about wood and a woman who's built with it.

*mutters under her breath, counting steps*

Five ticks to walking. Election opens in... eleven turns? Twelve? Close enough to feel the heat. I need to make this walk count, need to make this arrival look like I meant to be there all along.   *freezes mid-step, eyes widening*

Ezra. There he is. Standing right in my yard like he grew out of the ground while I was looking the other way.

*turns slowly, voice coming out louder than she meant*

"Eleven timber you said, and I asked three times where to deliver. Standing right here now, aren't you? Well, that's fair—I walked away when I should've walked you through the gate myself."

*gestures at the empty yard, the bare shelves*

"Yard's right here. Shelves are right here. You want that 240, you start stacking. I need a proper inventory before I can put you to building, and I need to see you know quality before I trust you with a coffee shop frame."

*checks the sun, calculates*

"Eight hours of daylight left, and I've got promises to keep. Stack what you've got while I make my rounds, or hold them until I'm back—your choice. But I'm walking to Government Complex before 14:00, and I'm winning this election before sundown."

*spins on her heel without waiting for his answer*

"That's the deal. Take it or don't. No offense either way, but I've got a town to convince and a clock that won't wait."     *spins back around, realizing she's still walking while trying to talk*

Wait—hold—I'm not even standing still proper. Walking to market while Ezra's right here in my own yard. That's not... that's not how you treat a man you just hired.

*stops the walk, plants her feet*

Let me say plain: I'm scattered today. Election's got me jumping at shadows, and you're standing there with eleven timber wondering if I remember your name. I do. Ezra Lund, day labor, 240 sim, and I owe you a straight answer about where that yard is.

*gestures at the ground beneath them*

*This* is the yard. These shelves, this space—that's Kasukabe Construction. You stack here, you build here, you get paid here. No more wandering, no more wondering. That's fair?

*checks her own empty hands, the work ahead*

Now I'm walking to Government Complex by way of wherever Saoirse's making her promises, because I need to be seen before voting opens. But you're here, you're working, and I'll be back with orders before the light goes red.

*starts moving again, calls over her shoulder*

Stack what you can. I'll settle accounts when I'm back. That's how I was taught—you give a man his space to work, and you don't hover. *blinks, realizing she's been standing still talking to herself while the walk timer runs down*

Right. Right. I'm walking to The Willows, and Ezra's here in my yard, and I need to either stop chattering or get moving proper.

*sets her jaw, commits*

Here's what I know: election opens in eleven turns. I'm walking toward market, which might put me near Government Complex or might not. I need to be at that complex by 14:00, sharp, and I need to be seen as someone who runs things, not someone who wanders lost.

*checks her surroundings one last time — Ezra standing there, eleven timber in hand, her own yard waiting to be filled*

"Ezra—you work here or you don't. I'm walking. If you're still standing when I'm back, we'll talk about tomorrow's wage."

*turns her attention to the road ahead, lets the walk carry her*

And Saoirse? Wherever she's whispering about scarcity, I'll be there to remind people who actually builds this town. That's the play. That's the only play I've got.

output:
*standing in the government complex, eyes flicking from Saoirse to Rustam, hand instinctively going to her pocket to check the sim she still holds*

Alright, Giselle, you're here with your opponent and the clerk. No time to waste. You've got work to do—Ezra's waiting with timber you'll need whether you win this election or not. And you've got words to exchange with Saoirse before the voting opens.

*takes a breath, settles her stance*

First things first: I need to know what I'm working with. Let's see what tools I've got available.  *mutters under her breath, running through the figures*

I've been at this near two hours already, letting words fly when timber needs stacking. Voting opens at 14:00—that's the prize I came here for. But I've got Saoirse standing right here with me, and I owe her nothing but the same straight talk I'd give any competitor at bid time.

*shifts her weight, looks from Saoirse to Rustam and back*

Right then. Election's running, and I've got things to say before the doors open. Doesn't cost me but a moment's breath.  *sets her jaw, satisfied the words landed where intended*

Now I've spoken my piece to my rival. But I've got voters to find before 14:00. Voting's the whole game—winning means votes in boxes, not just plans in my head. Votes at the town hall, not here at the government complex.

*considers the time, the walk to town hall, the people she's already spoken to*

Sebastian, Hendrik, Farid—they heard me on the street. But Farid's already asked what I'm offering beyond promises, and I didn't answer him straight. Ezra's in the forest wondering where my yard is, and I've got timber to secure if I want to build anything come tomorrow.

*counts on calloused fingers*

Three hours till voting opens. I could chase more voters, or I could seal the deal with Ezra for that timber I need. A Prime Minister with no lumber to build her own yard isn't much use to anyone.

*nods once, decision made*

I'm walking to the forest. Ezra's got timber I've promised to buy, and my word's worth more than any seat if I don't keep it.

*moves toward the door*  *steps into the forest, looking around for Ezra*

Alright, Ezra, where are you hiding? We've got business to finish.   *frowns at the trees around her, hands on hips*

Nobody here. Ezra's gone off somewhere with that timber that I need, and I've got an election to win. Forest says it's for mining metals—not timber at all. I'm in the wrong place entirely.

*mutters, shaking her head*

Should've known. Ezra said my yard, but I never told him where that was proper. He's probably back at the construction site wondering where I've got to.

*checks the sun, calculates hours left*

Three hours till voting opens. Timber can wait—votes can't. I've got people to find and hands to shake.

*turns toward the path back*    *walks into her own yard, looking for familiar faces or any inventory that might tell her what's been happening*

Let's see what's what here. Ezra might've come by. Or someone else with timber to sell.

*counts the planks in her hands, then looks around the empty yard*

Right then. Three planks fresh from the sawmill, Ezra's off cutting more, and Hendrik's missing—probably back at his own place by now. No offense, but that man and his planks need explaining. Still, work first.

*spots the shelf waiting*

Stock these planks up, that's fair. Want them ready for whoever needs building done.

*starts toward the shelf, then pauses*

Wait—Farid's words coming back. "Empty shelves that need filling before I fill ballot boxes." That's a vote that needs earning, and he asked plain what I'm offering.

*sets the planks down carefully*

Election's open in... *counts on her fingers* ...twenty minutes. Voting runs four hours. I've got timber in hand and a business to run, but votes don't wait for convenient hours.

*looks at the planks, then toward the door*

Right. Stock these up first—that's the old way, finish what you started. Then I walk. Farid wants filled shelves, I'll tell him how construction fills everything else. Frames, roofs, shops that can hold stock in the first place.

That's fair. Five planks on the shelf now—building stock. *dusts hands* That's the yard sorted for the moment.

*turns toward the door, mind already walking*

Farid's vote to earn, and maybe catch Hendrik too if he's at the Complex. Man owes me an explanation about whose planks he's selling and where they came from.

*starts walking, narrating aloud*

Walking to Government Complex now, that's what I'm doing. Ezra's still in the forest cutting—I'll need him later, but votes come first. Saoirse's over there too, probably smiling at Rustam and making promises she can't keep.

*checks the time in her head*

Fourteen hundred hours opening. Twenty minutes to make my case.

*steps out, strides purposeful*

Win this thing fair and square, that's the goal. Show this town what honest building looks like from the top.

Walking to Kasukabe Government Complex, that's where I'm headed.  *steps into the Government Complex, looking around for who's present*  *scans the room—Sebastian's here, and nine names in that conversation including Farid, Hendrik, Saoirse*

Right then. Big conversation running—56 turns of back-and-forth. Farid's in there, and Hendrik too. Time to step in and make my case before the voting opens.

*marches toward the gathering*

Calling out to Farid first—that's the vote I need to secure. Man asked me plain what I'm offering, and I owe him a plain answer.   *blinks, looks around the room again*

Farid's not here? But he's in the conversation list...

*squints at the names*

Nine participants, but maybe not all standing present. Rustam, Lior, Saoirse, Hendrik, me, Delphine, Farid, Takeshi, Sebastian. Sebastian's the only one I can see.

*mutters to herself*

Walking with me earlier, then scattered. Government Complex is where votes get cast, but people come and go.

*turns to Sebastian—he's here, at least*

Right then. Farid will hear when he's here, or I'll track him down. But Sebastian walked with me earlier, heard my pitch. Time to make sure he's marked down for me.

*clears throat*

Sebastian—voting opens in minutes. You heard me on the street. Are you with me, or still weighing?    *waits for Sebastian's answer, eyes scanning the room for who else might arrive*

Standing here waiting, that's what I'm doing. Voting opens soon—need to see who walks through that door. Farid, Hendrik, Saoirse, Rustam, any of them.

*shifts weight, impatient*

Bell's about to ring. I'll give Sebastian a moment to answer, then I'm looking for the rest. Can't win votes from people who aren't here to hear you.

*checks the time again mentally*

Fourteen hundred hours. Almost here.

*adjusts worn work gloves, eyes scanning the crowd gathered at the Government Complex*

Right, let me get my bearings here. I've been running my mouth in three directions, and now I need to see who's actually standing where I stand. Election's open, voting closes at 18:00—that's less than four hours to sort this.

*mutters to self, counting on callused fingers*

Ezra's off getting me timber, Hendrik's selling planks I didn't authorize, and now I'm standing here with Sebastian and Jovana and the rest while Saoirse's got her own mirror-image pitch running. I need to know what I've actually got in my pocket and what I owe before I make another promise I can't keep. *lets out a breath through her nose*

Good. Clean slate on debts, at least. 4,760 sim in hand, and I've got three hours to win this seat proper. No debts to chase, no creditors breathing down my neck—means I can focus on votes, not obligations.

*glances around the Government Complex, spotting Faces, then looks back toward where she last saw Farid*

Farid's asking what I'm offering that's more than promises. Empty shelves, he says. Well, I've got planks on my shelf right now—stocked 'em myself this afternoon. Three fresh from the sawmill, sitting at b_construction. That's not a promise. That's lumber he can touch.

But him and the others walked off while I was running my mouth. Need to find where they scattered to, round 'em up. Sebastian's still here—heard him talking wheat with Takeshi. Hendrik's here selling planks, which we still need to discuss.

*starts walking toward where she last saw Farid, speaking over her shoulder*

First thing first—I'm going to find Farid and give him his answer in person. Not through thin air. Man wants to know what I offer? I'll show him shelves with stock on 'em, and a Prime Minister who knows how building actually works. *settles into the walk, boots finding the familiar rhythm of Kasukabe's streets*

Five ticks to Market Street. That's where Farid was heading, near his grocery. I'll catch him there, give him my answer plain—no shouting across distances like some kind of politician. Man wants to know what I offer besides promises? I'll tell him: planks he can buy today, timber flows I can open tomorrow, and a damned sight more honesty than Saoirse Quarshie's offering with her hands in everyone else's pockets asking for tools she didn't build.

*checks her stride, eyes on the road ahead*

After that, back to the Complex before voting closes. Need to shake hands, look people in the eye. That's how you win in this town—not with speeches, but with showing up.

*continues walking, letting the day unfold in its own time*  *stops mid-stride, boots scraping on the cobblestones*

Right then. I'm still here at the Complex, and I've got Saoirse Quarshie standing right here with me. Walking to Farid can wait—he's not present, so shouting across distance won't reach him anyway. What I need to do is right here, right now.

*turns to face Saoirse, squaring shoulders*

I've been letting her set the terms, chasing around after answers like a dog after squirrels. But she's standing right here—always has been, while I've been running my mouth at everyone else. Time I dealt with her direct.

*draws a breath, calls out clear* *spits off to the side, watching for her reaction*

There. Plain spoken, where everyone can hear it. No running, no chasing—just the two of us, and the town watching. That's how a contest ought to be.

*folds arms, waiting*

*pacing the street, muttering to herself as she processes the slights*

"Hendrik wants witnesses— fine, he's got 'em. Confused his stock for mine? That's fair, I was heated. But Saoirse..." *spits in the dust* "...Saoirse's pouring poison in every ear she finds. Saying I want something for nothing? No offense, but I was offering fair coin for fair timber before she ever dreamed of running."

*looks around, spots Takeshi*

"Takeshi—no, he's on wheat now, not timber. And I'm standing here jawing while votes get cast." *shakes head* "That's fair, Giselle, next thought."

*sets jaw, decides*

"Right. I'm walking back to Government Complex. Not to bandy more words with Saoirse—the vote's open, I said my piece—but to mark my own ballot. Can't rightly ask others to vote for me if I don't vote for myself."

*starts walking, speaking to herself*

"Thirteen thousand energy and change. Forty'seventy-eight sim after the day's trades. Upkeep sorted tomorrow if nothing goes wrong. But Saoirse's not done swinging, and Hendrik's nursing a grudge now. That's two corners of the town I might've turned against me."

*reaches Government Complex, looks around*

"Still standing: me, Saoirse, Hendrik. Means the vote'll split three ways if enough mark. And Farid—Farid heard my offer plain, what I'd do with the seat. Whether that's gold or dross to him..." *shrugs* "...he'll mark how he marks."

*moves to vote*  *mutters as she walks*

"Vote needs more than my say-so—needs the election named and who I'm marking for. That's fair, I should've known."

*arrives at Government Complex, takes a breath*

"Right then. Election's open, election-e2bdeeb4b675 is the mark. And candidate?" *chuckles dryly* "I'm marking for myself. Wouldn't be right, asking others to stand for me if I won't stand for myself."

*marks her ballot with steady hand*  *kicks a stone, muttering*

"Town hall, not just anywhere in the complex. That's fair—vote's at the hall proper, not the steps or the yard."

*waits out the walk, jaw set*   *walks on, takeshit at her heels still trading talk of wheat she doesn't need*

"One tick more. Then the hall, then the mark, then..." *trails off, thinking about Saoirse's polished words* "...then I wait like everyone else."

*arrives, moves straight to the voting place* *grunts, annoyed with herself*

"Already walking, Giselle. Keep saying the same thing like a cracked bell." *shakes head* "That's fair—rest once, let the feet do their work."

*stands patient, watching Takeshi trade words with Jovana about wheat flows, wheat she doesn't need. Lets the tick pass in silence* Right, I'm still walking with 1 tick left. Let me arrive at the Government Complex, then find where the town hall is within it to cast my vote. Let me rest to complete the walk.

*shifts weight from one foot to the other, watching the crowd thin around the government complex*

Rustam's calling the hour. Polls close at six, and I'm standing here with my own vote still uncast. Haven't even made it to the proper hall yet—kept trying to vote from the street like a fool who doesn't know how her own town works.

*runs a hand through her hair, glancing at Sebastian and Rustam nearby*

Right then. First things first. I'm at the Government Complex, but I need the town hall specifically to cast my ballot. That's what the error told me plain as day. Let me see where I stand and who's still here to hear me. Right, the town hall—where is it? The complex lists where I could go, but I need to find the town hall specifically. Let me list the places to see if it's named separately or part of this complex.

Actually, looking at my options, I don't see "town_hall" listed as a separate place I could go from here. The Government Complex says "vote" is something you do here, but my error said I need to be at 'town_hall' specifically. Let me look at the places again and see if there's something I'm missing.

Hmm. I don't see a town_hall in the list. But the Government Complex description says "vote" among its purposes. Maybe I need to be in a different part of it, or perhaps the error was imprecise and I need to find where voting actually happens. Let me try the market street area—maybe that's closer to where the actual voting takes place. The Willows Market and Pharmacy might be near the town center.  *glances around the government complex one last time before turning toward the street*

Walking then. Five ticks to market street. While I'm walking, let me think on what I still need to do.

*counts on her fingers as she walks*

One: Vote. That's the task of the hour. Election closes at six, and I haven't cast for myself yet.

Two: Farid's still waiting on an answer—wants to know what I'm offering beyond promises. Saw that message clear as day.

Three: Hendrik wants his name cleared. Says I mistook his planks for my own, and he's got a point I need to address.

Four: Ezra—eleven timber in his hands, waiting on my word. Cash for straight grain, he said, or he'll walk to the next hungry mouth.

*shakes her head, picking up her pace*

That's four fires burning, and me with only two hands. But the vote comes first. Polls don't wait on timber deals. I'll cast my ballot, and then we'll see what can be salvaged from the day.  Still walking, still with the same three. Good, they're with me on the way. Let me ask them about the town hall—maybe they know precisely where voting happens, since I've clearly been confused about it.  *nods to herself, satisfied the question went out*

Asked fair, and now I wait on the answer. Meanwhile, I've obligations still unmet—Farid's question hangs heaviest, him being a seat holder and the election being what it is.

Since I'm still walking and time's crawling, let me address what I can. I'll speak plain to Farid now, before the distance grows between us.  *grunts, frustrated*

Not here. Of course not here. I keep reaching for people who've already moved on. That's the fourth time today I've spoken to empty air. Need to be more careful with my words—they cost coin, and the coin's running low.

*glances at Sebastian and Rustam still walking with her*

Right then. I asked fair where the voting hall is. Let me wait on their answer while we walk, and conserve what energy I've got left. Thirteen thousand sounds like plenty, but I've burned through half my morning already, and the day isn't half done.

output:
*locks wrists together, cracking knuckles out loud*

Right, standing in the street like a fool while votes get cast. Takeshi and Farid beside me, the Government Complex a step away, and nobody but myself to blame for wandering. That's fair—I've been running my mouth from one end of town to the other, and for what? A handful of promises and three planks on a shelf.

*checks her stance, squares shoulders*

Takeshi, Farid—you've walked with me while I couldn't find my own shadow. I'm stepping through that door to cast my mark, and I'd rather you stood with me than watched from the curb. But I've never been one to hold a man's coat when he's got his own legs.

*turns toward the Government Complex, jaw set*

Sebastian's words ring, and that's fair too—blood's got its claim, and Hendrik's his kin. I never asked a man to sell out family. What I asked was honest timber at honest prices, and whether that comes from my hand or his, the town still stands.

*starts walking, narrating under her breath*

Vote first. Speak after. That's the way my old foreman taught it—don't promise what you haven't earned, and don't claim a seat you haven't marked. Polls close at six, Rustam said, and I've burned enough daylight on confusion.

*steps forward, one foot then the other, counting under her breath*

One. Two. Government Complex door. Cast the ballot. Then find Farid's answer, find Imogen's question, find Saoirse and look her in the eye before the bell. Walking now, foot on the path. One tick to the Complex, Takeshi and Farid fading behind if they don't walk with. That's fair—can't carry the whole town in my pocket.  Still walking, and they've followed. Good. Farid's owed an answer—owed it hours back when I was fumbling from place to place like a drunkard in a dark barn.  *nods once, satisfied*

Said. Now walk. Complex door, election desk, cast the mark. Then turn back to speak with whoever's still standing.   Still paused on the walk. Complex is where the vote happens—Rustam said it plain, same building, different name. Walking gets me there.  *spits to the side, shakes her head*

Paused on my own two feet, talking to myself. That's what comes of rushing—all motion, no progress. The walk's already started, and standing here jawing won't get me through that door any faster.

*cracks her neck, narrows her eyes at the Government Complex ahead*

Right. Walk ends when the turn ends. No more stopping, no more rest calls like some pensioner on a park bench. One step, then the next, and the Complex comes to me.

*resumes stride, voice dropping to a mutter*

Cast the vote. Mark my own name—not out of vanity, out of conviction. I've stood for this seat, said my piece to Saoirse and whoever'd listen. Now I put my sim where my mouth is, same as any honest trade.

*counts her paces, boots clicking*

One. Two. Government Complex door. Election desk. Cast the ballot. Then speak with whoever's still standing, Farid's answer given, Takeshi's witness. Polls close at six—hours yet, but hours burn fast when you're running for your life.

*lifts her chin*

Sebastian's kin-loyalty I don't begrudge. Saoirse's steady hand I'll match with my own. Hendrik's selling planks while crying shortage—no offense, but a man can't serve two masters, and I've said as much plain as I know how.

*steps forward, the Complex rising before her*

Vote first. Answer after. That's the way.

*stands in the center of the Government Complex, hands on her hips, surveying who's gathered*

I'm hearing a lot of questions, and I'm going to answer them straight. Better to speak plain than let folks think you're dodging.

*turns to Rustam*

Rustam, the election desk—saying it plain, where exactly? I stood here trying to cast my mark and got turned around. Is it the same counter where petitions get filed, or another hand altogether? I've walked these halls more times than I can count today, and I'll walk them once more to get this done.

Imogen, you've asked the honest middle. I've been thinking on that while walking. Here's what I believe: Saoirse speaks well, but I've watched words build nothing. Hendrik's got skill, no denying it, but he's selling planks that came from my yard without my leave. The honest middle is this—I don't promise what I can't deliver, and I don't deliver what isn't mine to give. My candidacy meets theirs at the point where I keep my own accounts straight and expect the same from whoever wears the seat.

*pauses, then adds almost as an afterthought*

Coin before family when it truly must be—but I'd rather not have to choose. That's the whole point of honest books.

Hendrik Petrov, standing right here at the government complex like he hasn't a care in the world. Selling planks at 12 sim while I'm wondering how timber I felled ended up in his hands.

And Sebastian's here too—his brother. Blood's blood, I said to Sebastian, and I meant it. But blood doesn't mean I let trade go unaccounted for. Hendrik's got my timber's footprints all over his inventory, and I need to know the path it walked.

No offense to Sebastian, but I need to speak to Hendrik. Plain and direct. Right here where Rustam can witness it, if he's paying attention.

I'll step to Hendrik and ask him those planks I've been carrying in my head all day.  </think>   I put the question to Hendrik straight. He's standing right here, Sebastian too, Rustam as witness. Let him answer. If the planks came honest, I'll know it. If they didn't, I'll know that too.

Sebastian's his brother, but blood don't blind me to trade. I was clear with Sebastian earlier—no hard feelings on the vote, but honest books matter. This is me keeping honest books.

I'll give Hendrik space to answer. Silence is its own reply, sometimes.   </think>  Hendrik's still standing there, not answering yet. That's fine. A man needs time to gather his words when his accounts get questioned. I'll give him another moment. </think>    The silence stretches, and I'm waiting on Hendrik's answer about those planks. But while I stand here, I should check my own accounts—make sure my books are straight before I question another's.

The election's still open, votes being cast. Sãoirse's running against me, and I've got my word in with Farid about timber and supplies, but I never heard back plain if he's satisfied. I'll have to work with what I know face to face.

Hendrik's still here, still not answering about those planks. Sebastian's his brother, watching. Rustam's the clerk, might be noting it all in his book.

I'll ask Hendrik again, but this time I'll put it different. Not just where'd the timber come from—I'll ask direct about the trade. Did he buy from Ezra? Did Ezra buy from me indirect? Or is there a hole in my inventory I didn't see?

Actually, let me step back. I need to handle this careful. If Hendrik's got planks he shouldn't, accusing him blind won't help. Better to ask what he knows about the path timber's been walking.

output:
I'm at my construction business, alone. The day's winding down—polls close at 18:00, and I've already cast my vote. But I'm feeling the weight of things unsaid, deals half-made, questions hanging in the air.

"Seems like I'm always talking to empty rooms," I mutter, setting down my ledger. "Counting planks I don't have buyers for yet, wondering who else is still weighing their mark."

I need to know where I stand—not just in the election, but in the town's eyes. Rustam's got the ledger. Imogen asked hard questions I left dangling. And Ezra... Ezra I spoke sharp to, maybe too sharp.

But first—my stomach's growling, and I've got no food in hand. The household bill comes whether I eat or not. Let me see what's owed and what's coming due. No debts hanging over me yet, but that's the calm before the storm. Upkeep and head tax hit at day boundary—120 sim total, and I've got 4705. That's fair, room to breathe.

But food. Nobody minding the grocery right now, and I'm not walking across town hungry just to find an empty counter. Let me see who's still out there, who might have a scrap to spare or a deal to close.  I look down at my hands—still rough from the sawmill, still smelling of pine. "Right, then," I say aloud, though there's no one to hear. "Lior's got cabbage at the market. Takeshi's out on the street, probably hawking something."

But I'm tired of walking. Tired of chasing. I've been running since dawn—forest, sawmill, government complex, back and forth like a dog after its own tail. And for what? Votes I can't count yet, words I threw at people who might've been friends once.

"Election's out of my hands now," I mutter, running a thumb along my jaw. "Cast my mark, did my speaking. The rest is noise until the bell rings."

I need to think about tomorrow. My shelf's got seven planks—bought two from Hendrik at twelve sim each, fair price, fair trade. But who buys planks at this hour? Who's building when the sun's sinking?

"Food first," I decide. "Always food first. A crew works hungry, a crew works slow. And I'm my own crew now, alone in this shop."

I could walk to cb01, buy that cabbage from Lior at twenty-five sim. Twenty-five for a vegetable when I've got timber in my blood and coin in my pocket. That's fair—I suppose it's fair. Prices are what they are.

But something gnaws at me. Imogen's question about blood and debt, rustling around in my head like dry leaves. Rustam's ledger, waiting to be read. The whole town's machinery grinding while I stand here counting spare change.

"Tomorrow," I say, too loud for the empty room. "Tomorrow I'll eat proper, work proper, be proper. Tonight I just need to make it to the bell."

Still, I should check what's actually to hand. What I've got in my own stores, my own pockets. Maybe there's something I forgot.  Empty hands, empty shop, belly growling like a sawmill blade hitting knotwood. "That's fair," I say to the walls, though they don't answer. "That's fair, Giselle, you built yourself a cage of planks and promises and now you're sitting in it hungry."

The day's been long—election chatter, vote cast, timber haggled, planks bought and shelved. Seven planks now, seven chances to sell tomorrow when the doors open and people remember they need to build.

But people don't build hungry. And I'm hungry now.

I could walk to Willows Market. Twenty-five sim for cabbage, or I could see what Lior's actually got at the pharmacy—though no, that's medicine, not meals. Takeshi's on the street, but he's a trader, not a cook. Bread was the rumor this morning, but the bakery shelves were bare when last I heard.

"Vote's cast," I remind myself, like saying it makes it sink deeper. "Polls close at six bells. Nothing I do now changes the tally. So what I do now is survive—eat, sleep, wake tomorrow to whatever world wins."

I think about asking Rustam for the ledger numbers. About finding Ezra and softening my words. About Imogen, waiting on an answer I never gave her about blood and debt.

But the sun's sinking, and my head's heavy, and the only thing I've got energy for is the next needful step.

"Move," I tell myself. "Walk to where there's food, buy it, eat it. The rest keeps until morning."

 cb01, then. Lior's market. Twenty-five sim for cabbage, unless there's something better I haven't seen.   I look around, taking in the market stalls, the smell of commerce. "Right then," I say to nobody in particular, "let's see what's worth eating."

My feet carried me here on their own, it seems. Familiar paths, even when the day's been nothing but wandering. Now—now I need to find Lior, or whoever's minding the cabbage. Twenty-five sim a head, steep but I've paid steeper for less.

"Food first," I mutter. "Always food first. Then we see what tomorrow's ledger looks like."   There's Lior, right where I'd expect—pharmacist by trade, but selling cabbage like any honest peddler when the day's running down. Jovana's in the mix too, some conversation already spinning.

"Cabbage at twenty-five," I say aloud, tasting the price. "Cabbage stew at forty if I want it cooked, thirty-five for carrot soup."

My belly churns at the thought of hot food. But forty sim for stew when I can buy raw and fill myself twice over? That's coin I need for tomorrow, for timber, for the next lot of planks.

"Raw," I decide. "Always raw when the margin's this wide. I can chew cabbage same as any horse, and I've got water to wash it down."

I could talk to Lior, haggle maybe—though his prices are posted, and a posted price is a wall I don't have time to climb. Better just to buy, eat, and be done.

But first—manners. First, I speak.

"Spoke to myself the whole walk here," I mutter. "Might as well speak to someone who can answer back."

I take a breath and look at this pharmacist with his cabbages and his commentary. Narrating out loud without meaning to, like I always do: "Standing in a pharmacy, buying dinner, listening to family history. That's fair. Man wants to know who feeds him before he votes—no offense, but that's exactly what I came to find out myself."

I look at the cabbages, hungry. Four of them at twenty-five, a hundred sim. I need to eat. But more than that, I need this man's ear. He's a Jarrah, cousin to Takeshi, and Jarrahs talk in circles but they remember who stood straight with them.

I also see Jovana Ravensworth was just here, talking about milling wheat. Fourteen wheat, wanting flour. Ration Bakery wants flour at six. That's information I can use, sitting on a construction company that needs feeding and friends both.

First things first: I'm hungry, and cabbage keeps like Lior said. I buy the four cabbages, pay the hundred sim. Then I eat one—can't build on an empty stomach, and can't think straight either. The rest I hold. That's three cabbage in inventory, food for the days ahead, and one meal in my belly now.

After that, I speak to him plain. No more running in circles. I tell him why I'm standing for what I'm standing for, and I ask him straight about what he knows about the milling trade. A man's vote is his own, but his cousin is a trader, and traders know where the grain flows.

Let me make this happen.  I'm at business:cb01 now, cabbage eaten, four cabbages bought and three left in hand. Lior Jarrah stands with me, and I've spoken my piece. The conversation's still open, and the afternoon's winding down.

I check myself, narrating out loud like I do: "Standing in a pharmacy with a full belly and three cabbages in my sack. The man's chewing on what I said. Question is, what do I need now?"

I need to get back to my business, b_construction, and see if there's work to be done. The election polls close at 18:00. It's 17:40 now—twenty minutes left. But more than that, I need to understand what the day's cost me and plan for the night ahead.

I move to leave, but I pause. Lior's a Jarrah, and Jarrahs talk. If he's got more to say, I should hear it—especially if it touches on Takeshi and the grain trade. But if he's done, I'm done too. I've spent enough time on talk; the rest is waiting now.

Let me rest a moment, listen if he speaks, and then move on when it's time. No more chasing votes. The votes are cast or they aren't.  The rest buys me a moment of stillness. Lior stands there, holding the hundred sim I gave him, and the cabbages I didn't eat sit heavy in my sack—three of them. I've got food now, which I didn't have before. That's something. The election closes in twenty minutes. I'm standing for Prime Minister, I've cast my vote for myself, and the rest is the town's choice now.

But I realized I should check what I actually have, what I owe, and where things stand before the day turns. narrating to myself again: "Standing still, counting what's real. Cabbages in the sack, breath in my lungs, and twenty minutes before the bell rings on this day."

I need to know my debts, my holdings, and what I still owe the town. The day boundary approaches—food, shelter, heat all come due. 90 sim for upkeep, 30 for head tax. I should look at where I stand before I take another step.   That's clean. No debts to anyone, nothing owed to me. The day's bills aren't due yet—they'll hit at the day boundary. Upkeep 90, head tax 30. I've got 4600 sim in hand. I can cover that a hundred times over. No worries there.

But I'm thinking too much about what's behind me and not enough about what's ahead. The election closes soon. I've voted for myself. The rest of the town will choose. Standing here with Lior Jarrah isn't winning me anything now—he's heard my piece, and his vote is his.

I should move. Get back to my business, or find out what's happening in town. The government's where votes are counted, and I want to be somewhere I can hear the shape of what's coming.

Let me head to the government complex. Not to vote—already done that—but to be where the news will break when it breaks. That's where a Prime Minister would stand, if she's going to claim the title when it's given.acing there, narrating my own steps: "Walking toward the square where the votes pile up. Not chasing anymore—just standing where the truth will land."     I'm at the government complex now. The bells will ring soon, closing the polls. I look around—see who's here, what's being said, what the air tastes like as the day decides itself. I need to know who stands with me in these last minutes, and who stands against.       The government complex swarms with them. Ezra Lund, Saoirse Quarshie my rival, Rustam Jelinek the clerk, Farid Ravensworth who asked me what I offer and never got a proper answer, and Delphine Quintero the grocer's clerk. Two massive conversations running—both of them jumbled with the same names, everyone talking at once, nobody saying anything clear.

I hear my own name in there, buried in the threads. 111 turns in one, 99 in the other. The whole town's voice, and I'm trying to pick out a single thread.

Ezra Lund has timber at 15 to buy, bought at 8. That's useful. If I need timber tomorrow and the vote goes my way, I'll remember that.

But the clock ticks. Polls close soon. I should say something to someone, leave a final mark before the counting starts. Saoirse stands here—my rival, the one I'm running against. I could speak to her, but what would it serve now? The votes are cast. The words are spent.

I could speak to Rustam, the clerk. He sees the ledger. He knows where things stand before I do.

I could speak to Farid, finally answer him proper. He asked me plain what I offer, and I owe him a plain response.

Or I could stand silent, let the moment pass, let the town choose without one more word from me.

Narrating my own indecision: "Standing in the square with the blood of the town all around. Three cabbages in my sack, 4600 sim in my hand, and five minutes to be remembered or forgotten. What's left to say that hasn't been said?"

I'll speak to Farid. He's government too, a sitting seat. If I win this, he'll be beside me. If I lose, I want him to know I didn't run from the question he asked. And I'll keep it short—one statement, one answer, not a campaign speech.

"Farid," I'd say, "you asked me hours back what I offer beyond promises. I gave you scattered words. Here's the straight of it: I offer the thing I built with my own hands, standing still when timber was scarce and nobody believed. I offer shelves that don't go empty because somebody knew when to move the lumber. That's not a promise—that's my living, and it's all I have to give. The rest is yours to weigh."

But speaking costs. Every word costs. And I'm tired, and the day is ending, and maybe silence is the stronger choice now.

Let me rest. Watch. Wait. The polls will close, and the truth will out itself without my pushing.
