Rustam's talking ledgers at me like I'm hiding something. Well, the ledger's clean—I've got nothing against a clean ledger. But that third window business, and now he's standing here telling me about ballots while I'm trying to keep my business running and win a seat I already voted for myself in... No offense, but the man's got a way of making simple sound complicated.

Let me look around properly, see who's actually here and what needs answering before the day runs out on me. I've got Saoirse waiting on a response about timber and trading, and Hendrik wanting to know if I'm walking away from plank deals. Can't let both go cold. </think> Looking around to see who's actually standing here with me, and what's pressing. Need to get my bearings before the day runs out on me.  Saoirse's standing right here. She's the one I've been going back and forth with about timber and borrowing and trade. She said her piece about planks and carpentry and not borrowing, said it's the last she'll say on it. That's fair—she's got a right to defend herself. But I never called her a thief, not directly, and I need her to know that. More than that, I need these people here to hear me say it clear.

I'll answer her in the election conversation, the one that's been running all day. Let everyone hear me stand by my friend—not enemy, friend. Even when we're competing. Especially then. </think>  Answering Saoirse in the campaign conversation, where everyone's been listening. Need to make this clear.   That's that then. Said what needed saying. Now—I've got people here, connections to make before the day runs out. But I'm tired, true tired, and there's still that matter of Hendrik wanting to deal on planks. Let me rest a moment, catch my breath. Day's not over yet, and I've got cabbages in my hand and an election that'll decide tomorrow.  Resting here, catching my breath. Day's winding down but there's still work in it.       I'm still here at the complex, same faces around me. Rustam with his ledger talk, Farid waiting on an answer about what I offer, Ezra selling timber. And Delphine—new voice, young, just come into the conversation near the end. I remember what I said to her earlier, about learning by doing. Still true.

But I need to get back to my business. Construction yard needs timber, always needs timber. And I've got planks on the shelf now—seven, after stocking those two I bought from Hendrik. Need more, though. Always need more. 

First, let me check my debts before the day boundary hits. Don't want surprises.  Checking debts before the boundary falls. Don't like surprises when it comes to what I owe.   Clean. Nothing owing, nothing due. That's the way I like it. Now—timber. Ezra's here, selling at fifteen. That's steep. He's buying at eight, so he's looking to double his money. That's fair—man needs to eat. But I've got to run a business, and I need timber flowing at prices that let me build.

Let me talk to him, see if there's room to move. No offense, but fifteen's a squeeze on my margins.  Talking to Ezra about his timber price. Fifteen's steep for what I need.    Heard. Everyone heard. That's the way of politics—everything public, everything watched. I'm tired now, truly tired. Energy's running low, and I've got cabbages to eat before they spoil or the day takes them.

Let me eat one here, standing with these people. Don't want to show weakness, but a body's got to eat. Then—then I'll see what Ezra says, or if the day ends before he answers. Either way, I've made my stand today. Said what I believe, made my deals, kept my word where it counted.

That's all a builder can do. The rest is for others to judge.  Eating a cabbage, standing here. A body's got to eat, even in the middle of everything.

*muttering to herself as she processes the scene before her*

"So I'm standing at the government complex, seat's in hand, and I'm still answering questions from the morning's election. That's fair—people deserve answers, even if they already gave me their vote."

*narrows eyes slightly at the memory of the vote*

Already cast my mark, that I did. Held the line when Saoirse questioned my family's dealings. Wouldn't trade my cousin's name for political coin, no offense to those who'd expect it.

*turns attention to the present*

Now let me see what's what. Rustam's got questions natural for a clerk, Ezra's still sizing me up, and I've got two cabbage in hand with a household bill coming due.

*waves toward Ezra, addressing him directly*

Ezra—no offense, but you're buying timber at eight and selling at fifteen. That's a working double, and I respect the craft of it. I'll do business with a man who knows his margins, always have. The election's done for today, and I'm still standing here with my questions answered twice. Third time if you need it, but I'd rather talk planks than politics if you're selling.

*then turns toward Rustam*

Rustam—records are clean, you've said. 119 ballots, my name among them. That's the ledger's truth, and I don't question what the ledger holds. But you're a clerk with eyes wide—who's posturing for tomorrow if this one don't settle? You're holding more than stamps, or you wouldn't be standing here still.

*catches herself narrating aloud*

...and I'm talking at myself again, aren't I?

*settles into herself*

Giselle Ingram, construction's my trade, and I'm staying in the race until the bell rings or someone else carries it. That's all I know how to be.  *watching the four of them stand there, feeling the weight of 157 turns in this campaign conversation*

*glances at the government store within the complex*

...that's the margin I said I respected. Double's honest work.

*to herself, weary but standing*

*voice dropping to the ground, talking to the stones as much as herself*

Giselle Ingram does everything the way she was taught. That includes hearing what's said back before saying more. Ledger's quiet right now, and the clerk answers when he's ready—not when I push.

*takes stock of the energy running low, 12,653 now and the day still chewing through it*

Waiting's part of the job too. Always was. *still standing, breathing slow, watching the four of them like a foreman watching concrete set*

Silence costs nothing. That's what my old boss used to say—a man who couldn't read a blueprint but could pour a foundation square every time. I learned from him, even if he never knew what I couldn't do.

Got two planks in the construction yard. Two planks and a vote already cast. Whether it holds or crumples, that's the day's work done.

He's got the books. I just carry the weight.

Search tool's locked out on me. That's fair—I pushed too hard, too fast. And now Farid's walked, and Imogen's walked, and I'm standing here talking to empty air like a fool at a crossroads.

*spits to the side, quietly*

Saoirse's right there, though. Rustam too. And Delphine. Elections tomorrow, zero declared as of Rustam's last ledger-check. I need to know if Saoirse's standing against me, and I need to say my piece to these three still in earshot. No offense, but I don't walk soft when there's building to be done.

I'll ask Saoirse plain, and I'll tell Rustam what I think of his "contradiction"—my shelves aren't empty, I've got planks stocked, he's just not looking hard enough. And I'll deal with Farid and Imogen when I find them again, not before.

Delphine walked too. That's three people I tried to reach and missed—Farid, Imogen, Delphine. All scattered while I was standing still. No offense to myself, but I need to stop chasing shadows and deal with what's in front of me.

Saoirse and Rustam heard, though. Saoirse got my question plain: is she standing against me? And Rustam got my answer about the planks—seven on the shelf, bought honest, not the empty shelves he's imagining.

*runs a hand over my calluses, thinking*

The day's getting late. I've got two cabbages, 4587 sim, debts clear, and tomorrow's the election. Candidacy closes at 10:00, voting opens at 14:00. I've already cast my ballot, but I need to make sure I'm declared, and I need Saoirse's answer.

That's fair—the waiting's done, the working starts.  </think>  *stands still, shoulders set, breathing steady*

I'm here. Saoirse is here. Rustam is here. The day's running down—19:10 now, boundary coming, 90 sim for upkeep and 30 for head tax will auto-take. I'll have 4467 left, and two cabbages to get me through.

*low murmur, barely audible*

Waiting's the hardest part of building. The frame's up, the roof's waiting, and you can't do a thing until the lumber arrives. But when it comes...

*clenches and unclenches one fist, old habit*

When it comes, you work fast and you work true. That's what I'm doing now. Waiting for Saoirse's answer. Waiting to see if there's a fight tomorrow or if I'm standing alone. Either way, I'm building something this town needs—honest work, honest books, no more silence.

Hendrik's still owed a proper close on them planks, and Sebastian... blood's blood, and I said my piece.

Think now. What matters before the day ends?

The tax rate's at 300 bps—30 sim a head. That's government work, and I'm sat in that seat already, just Prime Minister needing papers filed. Could ease it down, give the town some breathing room before tomorrow's vote. Or could hold the line, show I'm steady.

Farid's the weight on my scale right now. 2348 sim, empty shelves, wanting my lumber piece. But he's not here neither—standing with Saoirse and Rustam now, from the sound of it.

I'll speak what's pressing, then walk where I need to be. Talking to myself again, and nobody here to hear it—just the walls and the ledger I can't quite read like I pretend to. Debts are clear, though. That's something. Still owe tomorrow—90 upkeep, 30 tax. Automatic at the boundary. No wiggle room in automatic.

I've got seats' powers at my fingertips. Could drop that tax, make life easier before polls open. Or could keep it steady, show I'm not buying votes with the treasury.

"Three hundred basis points," I mutter, running the numbers in my head, counting on my fingers like my father taught me. "Every man, woman, child—thirty coin a day. Not nothing. Not crushing neither."

Saoirse's got her play, and I know she's got numbers I don't. But I built this town's frames, rafter by rafter, and I'll be damned if I let anyone say I don't know what holds a roof up.

Hand's steady. Decision's mine. Drop it fair, for the people who'll stand in line tomorrow. That's standing by someone—give 'em breathing room before they mark their paper.  I look down at my own hand, surprised it moved without thinking out loud. "Two hundred basis points," I say to the empty hall. "That's twenty sim a head, not thirty. Took a third off the load before sunrise. That's fair—didn't promise nothing I didn't build myself."

The echo comes back to me. Nobody's here to know it yet, but the ledger knows. Day boundary, every household feels it lighter. Eighteen days I've had this seat, and I used it just now for something besides my own name in the book.

That's the weight off. Now I need to figure where the morning finds me. election's coming, and I'm standing in it.

"Polls open at ten," I narrate, walking toward the light from the window. "I need my name declared, my coin sorted, and my stomach fed before then. Two cabbage won't carry me through a campaign."

I could eat now—wouldn't make me less hungry tomorrow, but it'd make the walking easier. Or I could hold 'em, trade 'em, turn 'em into something stronger if someone'll buy.

The construction yard's got nothing on the shelf worth selling tonight. Planks I bought from Hendrik, milled and stacked. Nobody standing there to buy. But I've got a mind to check—see what's stocked, what's low, what's worth my time in the morning.

First, though, I eat. Can't build on an empty frame, and I learned that the hard way once. Never again.

I'm still standing here, money in hand, energy in my bones, and the night pressing down. Election's the mountain. This is just the foothills. The cabbage goes down, and I'm already thinking about the next meal. "One left," I say aloud, patting my belt where the lump of green sits. "Not enough for a working day, but enough to walk on."

The hall's empty, and I've spent my voice on air. Time to move, or time to rest. My legs know the way to the construction yard—they've walked it a thousand times.

But I'm tired now. Not the kind of tired that sleeps easy. The kind that wants to know what's waiting.

I stand still a moment, listening to my own breath. Then I decide.  Standing still, talking to myself about standing still. "That's the rest that costs nothing," I say, and nobody's here to hear it. "The government complex, empty as a church on Saturday. I've got words unpaid back to Hendrik, Imogen, Sebastian—sixteen hours of walking since I spoke 'em, and the debt still sits."

But I've done what I could. Tax rate's lighter now. One cabbage eaten, one held. Money in hand, energy in the tank. Tomorrow's the fight, and today's the footing.

"Close my eyes where I stand," I murmur, leaning against the wall, "or walk to where the work is."

The work's at the yard. The workers are home. The election papers wait for morning.

I'll move when I know where moving gets me. For now, I rest here, counting the echoes of my own voice against stone I helped raise.That's fair. That's fair. I say that when I know I've lost something, but can't say what out loud.

For now, the turn ends. The world turns with it. I'll see where standing got me when the sun comes up.

Election's tomorrow, the rolls are open till ten, and I've got timber waiting on men who've gone home. That's fair—show up when you say you will, leave when the work's done. I was taught that way, and I build that way. Anybody wants planks tomorrow, they know where to find me. Anybody's got questions for the seat, they can ask at the hall.

output:
I look around. Rustam and Imogen are still here. The town's winding down, but I'm not done yet. Election's tomorrow—candidacy opens at dawn, closes at ten. I need to be there when the doors open. Been too long playing catch-up on other people's clocks.

But first—there's work to do. Timber sitting idle doesn't earn, and I've got planks on my shelf that need company. I'm thinking I should get to my business, check what I've got, make sure I'm ready for tomorrow's trade no matter how the politics shakes out. Construction doesn't wait for election results.

I stand up, stretch my back the way my mother taught me, and start walking. Out loud, without meaning to: "Day's done when the work's done, not when the sun's down. That's fair."

I'm headed to my construction yard. Got to inventory what we've got, see what needs restocking, and sleep on-site if it comes to it. Being close to my materials, that's the old way. The way I was taught.  Good—I'm at my yard. Quiet here, like it always is after hours. Nobody around, nobody pricing, just the tools and the timber and the dark coming down. Out loud: "Planks at twelve, no bark on the price. Old way—no haggling after dark, no deals by lantern light. Sleep on what you can afford."

I need to rest. Day boundary's coming, bills will hit—90 for upkeep, 20 in head tax at the new rate I set. That leaves me... let's see, 4579 minus 110 is 4469. Still enough to work with. But I need energy for tomorrow. Election day's a long day, and I intend to win it fair.

The cabbage I eat now will keep me fed, but I should probably make use of the quiet. Rest here, sleep at my own place, be ready when the polls open. That's the old way. Show up early, stay till it's done.   Quiet out here. Just me and the planks stacked neat, tools hung where they belong. I never built this place, inherited it, but I run it the way it was shown to me. No shortcuts, no new tricks. If it worked for the ones before, it'll work for me.

Tomorrow I stand for Prime Minister. Against Saoirse—artisan, clever with her hands, probably clever with her words too. But running a town's not like running a loom. Takes more than craft. Takes knowing what's solid and what's just surface. I've been building this place, plank by plank, longer than most of them have been voting.

I eat the last cabbage, slow. Chew it proper. Then I close my eyes where I stand, back against the timber stack, same as I have a hundred nights before. Not pretty, not soft, but it's mine. That's fair.   Done. Last of the food, bills coming at the boundary, and me here with empty hands and full purpose. Tomorrow I win this election. Not because I'm owed it—nobody's owed anything in Kasukabe. But because I've built what this town stands on, and Saoirse Quarshie has only woven what drapes over it.

I rest. Let the night take what it will. Morning's when we build.

params.content: Rustam—desk'll keep till morning. Imogen—polls open at fourteen, and I'll be there with my name on the book. Anyone wants me tonight, they know where I build. Day's done when the work's done.

The work holds like frost until the sun returns. That's the way of things. Posted planks at fifteen, buying timber at ten. Sawmill's ready.  My door stays open. That's fair.

*standing in the construction yard, looking at the newly milled planks, checking my prices on the board*

Seventeen timbers now, seven planks on the shelf, prices posted fair. Day's closing. Ezra's grain walked to my wheels, and my wheels gave back fifty sim. That's the only payment I can trust—the one that crossed my own palm.

*muttering to the empty yard*

Ezra's still walking with his questions. Wheat to flour, barley to malt, and a wife's silence he can't square. Not my business. Not unless it walks into my yard with a bill I didn't charge.

Election tomorrow. Candidacy opens at ten, voting at fourteen. Saoirse Quarshie's name hasn't been called yet, and I need to know if she's standing against me. The Prime Minister seat's mine for now, but seats don't keep themselves warm.

*checking the ledger in my head, then the actual shelves*

Four thousand five hundred seventy-two sim. Timber bought at ten, planks sold at fifteen. That's the margin that keeps the lights on. No timber on the shelf to mill tonight, but seventeen waiting to be claimed.

*walking to the door, looking out at the street*

Farid Ravensworth wants his lumber talk. Best answers I have: can pay, can't pay, or will owe. No more silence, he says. Fair enough. But he's at the Government Complex, and I'm at my yard. Talk walks both ways, or it doesn't walk at all.

*pulling my coat tighter against the evening*

What's next? That's the only question worth answering.

I need timber. I've got the sawmill, the crew's gone home, but the mill doesn't sleep. Seventeen units waiting to be milled—craft them now, or wait for morning?

*rolls shoulders, looking around the empty yard*

"Solitude. Better than company that talks in riddles."

*checks the shelf, counts the planks with her eyes*

Seven planks at fifteen. Timber bid at ten. Ezra's got grain and questions, but he's walked to wherever the night takes men with grain. That's fair—I gave him my answer, he gave me his timber offer. The deal waits on morning.

Now. The election. Polls open at fourteen tomorrow, and I've got nowhere to stand but here. Saoirse Quarshie's in the race—I've seen her prices, furniture at one-fifty, flour at fourteen. Woman knows how to mark up. But I've got no timber coming in, and a sawmill that'll sit idle without it.

*spits in the dust, thinking*

First things first. I need to eat—three cabbages left, or that's what the world remembers. And I need to walk myself to where the governing happens, because this seat does me no good if I'm not sitting where the levers are.

But timber. Timber's the blood of this business. Ezra said he'd take ten per, and I've got coin to pay. Problem is, I'm here and he's... wherever men with grain go when the sun sets.

*checks her pockets, counts the sim again*

Four thousand five hundred seventy-two. Head tax takes twenty, upkeep takes ninety, that's one-ten gone before I wake. Enough to buy, enough to build, enough to bribe if it came to it. But I'd rather stand on my own feet.

Right. I'll walk to the forest. Not to fell—no axe in my hand, no energy to spare for swinging—but to see what's standing. To mark what needs cutting. Tomorrow, when the polls close and the votes are counted, I'll either be Prime Minister with a nation's timber to move, or I'll be Giselle Ingram with a sawmill and a debt to her name.

Either way, trees need felling.

*laces her boots, talking to the empty yard*

"Kasukabe Forest. One hour's walk, or that's what they taught me. Let's see if the old paths hold."  *spits on her palms, shouldering nothing but the weight of her own thoughts*

"Walking. Better than standing still and rusting."

*Five ticks. Forest holds timber, timber holds coin, coin holds the yard another day. She's walked this path before—first with her father's hand in hers, then alone, then with a crew that dispersed like morning fog. The forest doesn't remember. That's fair. It only gives what you take, and only if you've got the strength to take it.*

*checks her boots, loose lace trailing*

"Lace'll hold. Boots always held. Feet remember even when the mind wanders."

*strides into the dark between the trees, counting paces out of habit* Ezra! Good, she wanted to talk with him. And if there's an election soon... hmmm. She wants to be in power, but needs to play it smart. Keep walking, see what the terrain gives her. The forest isn't just trees—it's timber, it's coin, it's leverage. And Ezra, he wants something. Grain questions, wheat silences. Nothing comes free in Kasukabe.

output:
*mumbles to herself, boots crunching on street stone under the night sky*

"Walking home from the forest, that's what I was doing... and stopped for nobody. Empty street now. Good. Easier to think without mouths opening."

*shakes head, adjusts her coat*

"Upkeep's coming. 110 sim gone before I wake—90 for living, 20 for this head-tax I set myself at 200 bps. That's fair. I can see it both ways now: collector and collected."

*counts on her fingers, scowling*

"4561 minus 110 makes 4451, and the household food bill's still there tomorrow same as today. Two cabbages left, but that only feeds me if I eat them. Town needs building materials, not a full belly."

*spits into the dust*

"Ezra's words are still walking with me: Imogen silent, Hendrik paid, something sideways in the ledger. Wife won't speak where tax looms. No offense to Ezra, but that's his hearth not his business, and I've got my own yeard to mind."

*taps her work-worn palms together*

"Planks at fifteen sell, timber at ten buys. That's the spread that keeps the mill turning. seven planks sitting, and nobody tending. Business needs a hand on it come morning."

*looks up at the dark shape of the Government Complex, just passed*

"Election tomorrow—candidacy by ten, voting two to six. Saoirse's standing. I'm standing. And this seat I'm holding, Prime Minister with tax and rule in the hand, it goes to whoever wins the vote."

*slow exhale*

"Win against the odds. That's what I wrote. Wasn't supposed to be poetic."

*checks her pockets, her hold, her bearings*

"I'm at street, walking from forest I never reached. Supplies thin. Tomorrow's bills are certain. The vote's uncertain. That's two things I know."

*resumes her shuffle toward the construction yard, muttering*

"Keep doing what I was doing. That's all the old ways ever ask." *grunts at the refusal*

"That's fair—machine wants what it wants, not what I meant."

*shakes her head, muttering*

"Walking, then. One foot, then the other. Three more ticks to reach my own door, if I'm counting right."

*sets off again, boots steady on the stone*  *freezes mid-step, turns slowly at the shapes in the dark*

"Three of them. On the street, shadowed. Takeshi Jarrah—trader, cousin to Lior the pharmacist. Imogen Lund—Ezra's wife, wheat silent, tax looming. Delphine Quintero—grocery clerk, standing with questions."

*voice dropping to a growl, hand instinctively checking for her purse*

"Keep walking to the forest, that's what the machine thinks I'm doing. Never mind I changed my mind ten turns back. Road's long, night is longer, and company on a dark street means one of two things."

*steps back against the wall, shoulders set*

"Speak first or wait to be spoken to. That's the choice. And I'm too old to wait."  *nods once, jaw set*

"Heard. Three witnesses, one voice back. That's how these things start."   *folds her arms, weight on one hip, waiting*

"Still walking, the machine says. Still moving toward a forest I don't need. I'll stand here until someone answers, or until the dark gives up its secrets."

*spits to the side*

"One of us will break first. I've learned: it's rarely me."
